"Well," Gabriel said.

"Yeah," Imani said.

Elena and Arun were waiting in the receiving corridor. Their coveralls were clean — they had been working inside, where everything was controlled and predictable. Both had the posture of people who had been reviewing data all day and had come to the same conclusion independently.

"Imani." Elena's voice was neutral — the neutral of a commander who had not yet decided whether to frame this as a setback or as data. "Full debrief in the lab in twenty minutes. Bring the cores."

"Understood."

Arun stood at Imani's elbow when she stepped from the rover cabin, his eyes going past her to the two sample tubes sitting in their foam cradles. "You found moisture. Three to seven percent. That's what the relay data showed before signal degraded."

"That's what we found." Imani removed her gloves one finger at a time, the way people removed armor after a battle that had not been a disaster but had not been a victory either. "Two meters, three meters. Both cores were moisture-bound regolith. No free ice. No lenses. No crystals. Just damp soil."

Arun nodded slowly — the acknowledgment of an engineer who had expected one thing and received another, and was already recalibrating. "The orbital radar showed high reflectivity at three meters. We saw the bands. We tracked them along the transect."

"Maybe the bands were hydrated minerals, not ice. Maybe the radar was reading something that looked like ice but wasn't."

"Or maybe the ice is there and we didn't drill at the right spot." Arun's voice was clinical — the voice he used when discussing systems that had not performed as designed. "We drilled two points in a zone the orbital data covered at maybe fifty-meter resolution. The ice could be thirty meters to our left. We wouldn't know."

Elena's expression was carefully neutral, but Gabriel, watching from behind his recorder, saw the tightness around her mouth. They had been counting on water. The imported reserves were finite. The water board in the mess hall — a whiteboard with numbers everyone looked at and no one discussed — showed a projected depletion date that had not moved. Every expedition that came back without ice pushed that date closer.

"Twenty minutes," Elena said again, and turned away.

Imani walked with Arun toward the lab, carrying the sample tubes in a padded case. Gabriel followed, documenting the walk of two people who had returned from twelve kilometers of ground with damp soil and a lot of questions the answers so far did not satisfy.

Behind them, the convoy parked itself. The crew who had stayed behind unloaded equipment haulers and watched the telemetry screens replay in their heads — the same thing everyone had seen: a drilling operation that had produced data, but not the data they needed.

In the corridor outside the mess hall, the water board sat on its hooks, and the number for imported reserves had not changed. Because it wouldn't change until someone drilled into actual ice and pumped it in. Until then, the same number was the worst kind of number — one that reminded everyone every day that time was passing and nothing was moving.

---

## Scene 2

The lab was full — not just with people who needed to be there for the technical debrief, but with people who needed to hear the outcome so they could adjust their own expectations on a colony where both time and energy were scarce.

Elena stood at the front of the room with tablet in hand. Thirty people assembled — every able-bodied adult in the base, because on a colony this size, a debrief on water was not a departmental meeting. It was a colony-level event.

Imani stood beside Arun at the assay table, the two sample tubes side by side in their foam cradles. The material inside was a uniform dark reddish-brown, slightly darker than surface dust, visibly damp.

"We drilled at two locations within the high-reflectivity zone," Imani began, her voice flat with the professionalism of a field operator reporting results she knew would complicate everyone's day. "First hole at two meters: moisture-bound regolith. Water content approximately three to four percent by mass."

She let the number settle. Three to four percent sounded like a lot until you realized extracting it meant heating every kilogram of soil to drive off adsorbed water molecules, and the energy cost was roughly twenty times the cost of melting ice.

"Second hole at three meters: moisture-bound regolith. Five to seven percent by mass. Slightly wetter. Suggests a moisture gradient — increasing with depth. But still bound water. Still not ice. Still not in a form we can efficiently extract."

Arun stepped forward. "I ran the energy models for extracting bound water at this concentration," he said, with the carefulness of an engineer presenting a calculation everyone already suspected but no one had wanted to hear aloud. "Thermal processing of regolith at three to seven percent requires approximately six thousand kilojoules per liter of recovered water. Melting clean ice requires approximately three hundred. The bound water route is roughly twenty times more energy-intensive. At our current surplus generation of one hundred sixty kilowatt-hours per day, processing regolith yields approximately seven to eight liters per day — below the minimum physiological requirement."

A silence fell. The math was not debatable.

Then Jonah spoke from the back, his voice carrying the blunt frustration of a man who had spent weeks preparing equipment for an extraction run that had produced nothing worth extracting.

"So what are we supposed to do with this?" Jonah asked. "I've got the crew building habitat modules. I've got robot maintenance schedules, repair queues, structural reinforcements. Every robot I assign to prospecting is every robot I'm not using for construction. And the ground keeps telling us it doesn't have what we need."

He didn't say *I told you so*. He didn't have to.

Sofia Vasquez stood up. "Jonah, the orbital data wasn't fabricated. The orbital survey detected high-reflectivity bands. The bands were real. What they represent — ice, hydrated minerals, cemented regolith — that's what ground truthing is for. We sent a convoy to find out. We found out the orbital data was ambiguous. That's not a failure. That's the point."

"The point was to find water," Jonah said. "We found damp dirt. Now I've got two fewer robots for the next three days because Tomas has them running survey transects for another site that might also produce damp dirt."

Tomas, near the door with arms crossed, looked up. He spoke with the same methodical precision he used to program rovers — deliberate, measured, unflinching when the data went against someone's preferences.

"The robots are not your property, Jonah. They're colony assets. And the most critical shortage on this colony is not habitat space — it's water. Imported reserves are finite. Every day without local water production is a day closer to depletion. If you want to debate priority, let's debate it. But in Elena's office, not in a lab."

Elena raised her hand. Small gesture, absolute weight.

"That's enough." Her voice was quiet but carried the full authority of the room. "We are not going to sit here and argue about whose work matters more. Jonah, your work matters. Tomas, your work matters. Imani, your work matters. Every person in this room is working on a problem that, unsolved, threatens this colony. The question is not whose problem is more important. The question is how we solve all of them with the resources we have."

She looked around the room, making sure everyone felt both the weight and the fairness.

"I'm ordering a broader subsurface survey. Not just the site near Drill Site Alpha. Multiple sites. Different coordinates. Broader coverage. The orbital data covered this whole sector, and we've tested one point. That's not enough to declare the region dry, and it's not enough to commit to it either. We need more data points before we decide where to focus extraction."

She turned to Tomas. "Three robots for surveying, not two. I want GPR transects at five additional locations within a twenty-kilometer radius. Spread them out. Flat plains, slope gradients, ancient channel features. Data compiled and reviewed within seventy-two hours."

Tomas nodded. "Understood."

"Imani — you lead ground validation. When the survey identifies promising sites, you deploy the drill. Two holes per site. Resource discipline."

"Yes, Commander."

"Arun — keep running energy models for both scenarios. Ice extraction and bound water extraction. If we find ice, we're ready. If we don't, we know exactly what bound water processing costs."

"Already on it," Arun said.

She turned to Jonah. "I know the reassignment impacts your construction schedule. Work with Tomas to find a schedule that serves both. I don't care if it means night cycles, staggered windows, or double shifts. Find the overlap. We don't have the luxury of treating these as separate problems."

Jonah held her gaze, then nodded — not enthusiastically, but without argument. "I'll coordinate with Tomas. But I need a firm timeline on when I get the robots back."

"You'll get them back when the survey is complete."

Elena lowered her hand. The room was quiet — not the silence of agreement, but the silence of people given direction, processing what it meant.

"We keep looking," Elena said. "Because the alternative is accepting we have no local water, and I am not prepared to accept that until the data tells me it's true. Until then, we survey, drill, analyze, and adjust. That's the process."

She stepped away. The briefing ended. The work continued.

Gabriel watched the crew file out, recorder running, capturing the sound of thirty people dispersing into corridors, each carrying a slightly different understanding of what had just happened. Some would leave frustrated. Some purposeful. Most tired. All of them would look at the water board on their way out and see the same number, and know it hadn't moved, and know it wouldn't move until someone found ice and brought it home.

---

## Scene 3

The lab emptied slowly. Imani cataloged the sample tubes — labeling with coordinates, depth, time, assay results. Arun packed the portable assay lab, wiping down instrument surfaces to remove the fine red dust that had infiltrated despite containment protocols.

Gabriel stayed behind. He was watching Mei, who had remained seated at the far end of the assay table, her hands resting on the edge, expression contemplative.

Mei Okoye was the colony's biologist and greenhouse manager. She had landed with seed banks and a research plan assuming reliable water access within six months. That assumption was now seven weeks old and showing strain.

Her greenhouse housed approximately two hundred plants — wheat, soybeans, lettuce, tomatoes — each a data point in the question of whether terrestrial biology could survive in a controlled Martian environment with recycled air, LED lighting, and a power budget counted to the kilowatt-hour.

The plants were stressing. Mei had told Gabriel two days ago that the recycling loop wasn't providing enough irrigation for the density she'd established. Younger transplants were wilting. Lettuce yellowed at the edges. Tomatoes had stopped flowering. She was rationing water between plants, prioritizing those closest to maturity and sacrificing the rest — a decision a biologist made with the same heavy pragmatism a commander made choosing which missions to fund.

She looked up as Gabriel approached, and her expression shifted — from isolation to willingness to share.

"Gabriel. Still recording."

"Always."

"Sit." She gestured to the chair beside him.

For a moment, neither spoke. Lab hum — environmental systems, assay diagnostics, Arun packing in the next room.

Mei looked at the two sample tubes. The dark soil inside visible through the clear walls.

"Bad data," she said quietly.

"Not bad data," she corrected herself. "Good data that points to a bad situation. That's different."

"Is it?" Gabriel asked.

Mei's hands moved on the table — not nervously, but the way a biologist's hands moved when thinking in systems and processes.

"Bad data is wrong data. Broken sensor. Contaminated sample. Recording error. If the drill malfunctioned and cores were contaminated, that's bad data. This" — she picked up a sample tube, turned it in her hands — "is good data. The sample is what it is. The assay is accurate. Orbital predicted ice. We found bound moisture. That tells us something true about this specific location. Good data."

"But it points to a bad situation."

"It does. Because good data can still produce bad outcomes. Good data tells you exactly what the problem is, and the problem can still be that you're running out of water, and the solution is still somewhere beneath ground you haven't tested."

She set the tube back and looked at Gabriel. In her eyes, he saw the same fractional tightening he'd seen in Imani's face in the rover — truth weighed against morale.

"Good science is asking the right question and getting an honest answer. Survival is the outcome you need. The two are not the same. You can do everything right — design the experiment, collect the data, analyze honestly — and the answer can still be 'no ice here.' Survival doesn't care that your methodology was sound. Survival cares about the answer."

She paused.

"I am looking at two hundred plants dying because I don't have enough water. I'm not asking whether the data was good. I'm asking whether it tells me where the next liter is coming from. Right now the answer is no. The data tells me where it's not coming from. Which narrows the search — useful — but it's not the answer I need."

Gabriel nodded. He was already writing the passage in his head for the Founding Record: *On Mars, the distinction between good science and helpful answers isn't academic. It's the distinction between knowing you're wrong and knowing how to be right.*

"So what do you do? When good data produces a bad outcome?"

"You accept it. Don't argue. Don't pretend. Take the honest answer — no ice here — and refine your next question. Not *where is the ice.* Too broad. The question is: where is ice within twenty kilometers, at drillable depth, with affordable energy cost, at justifiable concentration? Answer that with more data. More transects. More drill holes."

She looked at the tubes once more.

"People don't understand that 'no' is a valid answer. 'No ice here' isn't failure. It's elimination. You eliminate one possibility, you're closer to the next. But elimination doesn't produce water. It produces a smaller search area. And when your plants are dying, a smaller search area doesn't feel like progress. It feels like delay."

"Are your plants going to die?" he asked.

"Some. Yes. The deprioritized ones — late-stage transplants, weaker seedlings. I don't have the water. I've already removed forty plants. Composted them. Fed organic matter back into the growth media. Not waste if you cycle it. But I can't cut more without eliminating entire crop varieties. No tomatoes, no lycopene source. No soybeans, no nitrogen fixation. So I keep them at minimum water, and some survive, some don't."

She stood. Gabriel stood with her.

"I need water, Gabriel. Not for a better greenhouse. Because the greenhouse is the beginning of food independence. Every surviving plant is a step away from import dependency. And dependency on a supply chain a hundred million kilometers away is the most fragile dependency that exists."

She picked up a tray of seedlings — young, fragile, green things out of place against Martian soil and metal instruments.

"These are wheat. First generation of Martian-grown wheat. Parent plants grown from Earth seed. These seedlings grown from Martian-grown seed. Genetically identical to Earth wheat. But environmentally, already different. Higher CO₂, LED lighting, recycled water, processed Martian soil. They've never experienced Earth. In every practical sense, they're Martian plants."

She held the tray carefully — the way a priest holds something sacred, not because she was religious, but because context defined ordinary and extraordinary, and here, a tray of seedlings was the most extraordinary thing on the planet.

"I need water for them. Not for the experiment. For them."

She walked out carrying the tray, and Gabriel watched her go, recorder capturing the sound of footsteps — light, careful, carrying something fragile through corridors built for people used to being strong.

When the lab was empty except for him and the two tubes, Gabriel sat and looked at the dark soil. Damp dirt. Good data. Bad outcome. Mei had framed it perfectly, and he would use her framing because honest was the only thing the record demanded.

*Good science can still produce bad outcomes when the question is survival.*

He spoke the words aloud and let the recorder capture them. Not his words. Mei's. True for all of them.

---

## Scene 4

The robotics bay had been reorganized three times since landing. First: deployment — getting every robot operational. Second: maintenance — repairing dust damage, replacing joints, clearing sensor housings. Now: assignment, which was a zero-sum game.

Tomas stood at the planning console — a large touchscreen showing the colony's twelve-robot fleet as colored icons on a schematic. Blue: active. Yellow: maintenance. Grey: offline. Red: beyond field repair. Nine operational. Three down.

Colored icons moved between zones: Construction, Prospecting, Maintenance, Reserve.

Three robots in Construction: a heavy-loader, a general-purpose utility, a maintenance unit. The robots Jonah needed for habitat build-out — lifting components, welding joints, moving insulation panels.

Two in Prospecting: a scout, a heavy-loader. The robots for survey and drill support.

Tomas moved one icon from Construction to Prospecting — the second general-purpose utility unit, the versatile machine Jonah used for automated assembly of habitat module junctions, requiring precision welding no other robot could manage.

The bay door opened. Jonah entered without knocking. On a colony of thirty, knocking was formalism no one afforded.

"Tomas," Jonah said.

Tomas had seen him on corridor cameras. He knew this conversation.

"I'm reassigning Utility-2 to prospecting," Tomas said.

"Utility-2 is on module junction assembly," Jonah said. "We're three junctions behind schedule. Eastern corridor expansion stalled. Every EVA we do instead of robot welding exposes someone to radiation, cold, risk."

"I know."

"Do you?" Jonah stepped to the console. "Utility-2 is the only robot with precision manipulators for structural welding. Heavy-loaders lift. Scouts survey. Maintenance units inspect. But only Utility-2 welds. And you just moved it from the one task nothing else can do."

Tomas turned from the screen. Two men not enemies — colleagues small enough in number to know each other's work, large enough in responsibility not to always understand each other's constraints.

"Commander Varga ordered a broader survey. Five additional sites. GPR transects. Ground validation. Two drill holes per site. Seven locations. Each requires robot support for deployment, sampling, recording."

"You have two scouts and a heavy-loader."

"Scouts pull GPR but can't set up drill masts. Can't manage sample tubes. Can't operate assay labs. They don't have manipulators or processing power beyond movement and sensing. Heavy-loader carries but doesn't operate tools. We need Utility-2 for tool operation at the drill site."

"I need Utility-2 for welding at the junction site."

"I know."

"Then what do you want me to do, Tomas? Stop building? Because one robot means I'm back to human EVA for everything that requires precision work. Exposing people to risk for jobs a robot should do."

Tomas's voice was steady — the same tone he used when explaining robot specifications to people who wanted machines to do things they weren't designed for.

"The colony's physical footprint matters. But water matters more. Without local water, we don't have a footprint beyond four months. We can build corridors and junctions, but if the water runs out, the crew is dead. That is not hypothetical. It's mathematical."

He paused. Jonah heard the same calculation he'd been making himself since the convoy departed.

"I'm not taking Utility-2 because I don't care about construction. The order has priorities, and water production is highest until the depletion date moves. When we find ice, Utility-2 goes back to construction."

"How long?"

"Tomas."

"How long, Jonah. How long do I plan for before I get it back?"

Tomas calculated. "Five sites. GPR: twelve hours each, mostly autonomous. Ground validation and drilling: eight hours each. Two sites in parallel — survey complete in three to four days. Utility-2 reassigned at end of survey."

"Three to four days. Minimum."

"Minimum."

Jonah exhaled sharply. "Fine. But when the survey is done, Utility-2 comes back. Not 'when convenient.' When it's done."

"I promise," Tomas said. Simple. Direct. On a colony this size, as binding as a contract.

Jonah nodded and turned toward the door.

"Jonah," Tomas said.

Jonah stopped.

"I know it hurts the build-out. I know you're working against a compressed schedule. I'm not asking you to be happy about this. I'm asking you to trust the priority is correct."

Jonah looked back at Tomas, then at the screen, then at the floor. "I trust the priority. I don't trust the ground. The ground has lied to us once."

He left. The door closed. Tomas turned to the console, his hand near the icon representing Utility-2 — a machine about to spend three days pulling ground-penetrating radar across untested terrain, looking for something orbital data had suggested but could not confirm.

Tomas did not hope. He programmed, tested, deployed, monitored. But if the robots had emotions, he thought, they'd be hoping too.

---

## Scene 5

The survey ran three days.

Tomas deployed three robots across five sites within twenty kilometers of the base. Each site selected by orbital reflectivity, terrain characteristics, and geological features suggesting possible ice: ancient channel beds where water may have pooled, slope gradients where ice lenses could form, flat plains with layered moisture-trapping material.

The robots moved with the determined purposefulness of machines that didn't know discouragement. Scout Alpha and Bravo pulled GPR frames in parallel, their sonar painting subsurface cross-sections, sending data back through the relay satellite in staggered bursts. Utility-2 operated the assay lab at each site, conducting on-site moisture analysis of shallow cores, providing initial data before drill deployment.

Imani monitored from the base, sitting at the telemetry console in communications, watching data accumulate with the focused attention of someone reading a story written in radar reflections.

Gabriel sat beside her, recorder running, capturing the quiet drama of a survey that — unlike the first expedition — carried no buoyancy of orbital optimism. This run was grounded by terrestrial skepticism. They went out knowing the ground had already disappointed them once and could easily do it again.

Day one: Site Two returned results similar to Alpha — moisture-bound regolith at two to three meters, four to six percent, no free ice. The orbital signature had been strong; the ground truth was the same. Imani logged it without comment. Expected it. Prepared for it.

Day two: Site Three and Four both negative — dry regolith at all depths, moisture below two percent, indistinguishable from surface dust. The orbital data had flagged them medium-probability. The ground revealed them as essentially sterile.

Tomas adjusted the plan, reprogramming the robots to focus on Site Five — the last untested location, fourteen kilometers northeast, where orbital data showed the second-strongest ice signature in the sector. Site Five sat at the edge of an ancient channel deposit — a shallow depression where orbital imaging suggested water had flowed billions of years ago during a warmer phase of Mars' history. If ice existed in this sector, Site Five was most probable.

Evening of day two, Scout Alpha completed its GPR transect across Site Five. Data began arriving.

Imani was running on cold coffee and the focused exhaustion of fourteen hours at a console. Tired eyes, sharp attention — the sharp that comes from knowing one bright band on a waterfall plot could change everything.

The first transect populated — wireframe cross-section, color-coded reflectivity map she'd been reading since the first expedition.

She leaned forward.

Top layer: fifteen centimeters loose regolith, dry, low-density. Compact layer below, also dry. But below that — two meters deep — there was something.

A band of high reflectivity. Stronger than anything at Alpha. Stronger than any site in this survey. Continuous, not patchy — a coherent layer running parallel to the surface for at least thirty meters, signal strength unmistakable.

This wasn't hydrated minerals. This wasn't cemented regolith. This was ice.

Imani felt the thing in her chest — same as at Alpha but stronger, because she'd seen the ground refuse her three times before giving her something worth feeling.

"Gabriel." Her voice was steady, but something underneath it — a current, a hum — the sound of someone standing on the edge of a result that might matter. "Come look."

Gabriel moved to her side. The recorder tracked the screen — the bright continuous band at two meters, the signal strength exceeding every threshold, the clean signature saying clearly: *water is here*.

"That's strong," he said, because the word *ice* felt too committed. He'd seen orbital promise before. Watched ground refuse it. He wouldn't make the mistake twice.

"Much stronger." She pulled up the amplitude comparison — side-by-side rendering of Alpha and Site Five. The difference was not subtle. Site Fifty's reflectivity was roughly twice as strong, with broader spatial distribution.

"Mission AI, compare Site Five returns to orbital predictions."

"Comparing. Site Five reflectivity amplitude is approximately eighty-seven percent above orbital prediction for this location. Orbital data underestimated ice content significantly. The ground is wetter than predicted."

"Wetter," Imani said. She let herself say it because the data supported it, and she'd learned that on Mars, you said what the data said and nothing more.

She stood — legs stiff from fourteen hours — and keyed the colony-wide channel.

"Commander Varga. I'm at telemetry. We have a result at Site Five."

Elena responded in under thirty seconds — she had been awake monitoring, as she always was during active survey.

"Go ahead, Imani."

"Site Five GPR shows a strong, continuous high-reflectivity band at approximately two meters depth. Signal amplitude is eighty-seven percent above orbital predictions. Not bound moisture. Consistent with discrete water ice at significant volume. I recommend ground validation."

A pause. Two seconds — shorter than expected.

"Understood. Convening the team at oh-seven-hundred. No public announcement — I want confirmation before anyone adjusts expectations." She paused. "Imani — good work. All of you."

Channel closed. Imani sat back down and for the first time in three days, let herself feel the thing in her chest without setting it aside.

Not joy. Not triumph. The quiet satisfaction of a hypothesis surviving contact with evidence — the feeling when the ground, after refusing three times, finally said *yes*.

Gabriel sat beside her, recorder capturing the quiet of the bay, the hum of servers, the vibration of environmental systems cycling through the night, and underneath it, the sound of a woman who had been right to keep looking.

"Site Five," she said quietly, to no one, to herself, to the ground fourteen kilometers away keeping its secret just a little longer. "We're coming. And this time, we're not coming with illusions."

She pulled up the drill deployment plan and began the pre-mission checklist — vehicle status, drill calibration, sample tube inventory, rover batteries, EVA suit inspections. The work of preparation, carrying them back to the site where the ground had finally answered, the work of people going back out with fewer illusions and more instruments, and the stubborn, technical, unglamorous hope of those who'd learned that Mars didn't give you what you expected.

But sometimes, if you asked enough times, it gave you what you needed.

---

*End of Chapter 11 — Bridge: They go back out with fewer illusions.*

## Scene 1

Arun sat in the engineering bay at oh-three-hundred, which on Mars was not midnight but simply the hour most people were asleep in their bunks, their breathing monitored by the same environmental sensors that tracked every other parameter of the colony's survival. The bay was quiet except for the steady hum of the reactor cooling loop and the soft clicking of relay switches cycling through automated checks on the power distribution grid.

He had a tablet on his knees and a sheet of engineering graph paper on the workbench beside it. On the tablet, Mission AI had compiled the oxygen budget — a spreadsheet of inputs, outputs, reserves, consumption rates, and projected timelines that Arun had asked for that afternoon and that the AI had delivered with the cold precision of a system that had been running the same calculation for three months and had watched the projected end date creep closer with each passing cycle.

He had transferred the numbers to graph paper because some data needed to be physical. Screens could be closed. Graph paper could not. A sheet of paper on a workbench was a statement: this problem is not hypothetical, it is not theoretical, it is not something I will deal with later. It is here.

The numbers were straightforward.

Oxygen storage: eight hundred forty liters across four pressurized tanks, each holding approximately two hundred ten liters at standard temperature and pressure. The tanks had been imported with the original supply cargo — heavy steel cylinders, painted a faded blue that made them easy to identify in the dimly lit storage module. They were the colony's breathing money. When they were empty, the colony stopped breathing.

MOXIE output: approximately three hundred liters per day. A MOXIE unit — Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment — was a device that used solid oxide electrolysis to split carbon dioxide from the Martian atmosphere into oxygen and carbon monoxide. The technology had been proven on the Perseverance rover in the 2020s, where a single MOXIE unit produced approximately ten grams of oxygen per hour, enough to sustain a human for about ten minutes. The colony had brought two full-scale MOXIE units — larger, more efficient versions designed to produce oxygen at a rate that could sustain a crew of thirty, assuming the system operated continuously and nothing broke.

Current MOXIE output: approximately three hundred liters per day. Not the design target of approximately four hundred fifty. The shortfall was due to a combination of factors — one unit with a degrading electrolyte membrane, another running below optimal temperature because of thermal management constraints in the shared workshop space.

Oxygen consumption: approximately nine hundred liters per day for thirty people at rest and light activity. The number fluctuated with workload — EVA days consumed more, sleep cycles consumed less — but the daily average was stable, and the daily average was what mattered.

Three hundred liters produced. Nine hundred consumed. Deficit: six hundred. Reserve: eight hundred forty liters, declining at six hundred per day, lasting approximately fourteen days.

Fourteen days. Two weeks. On Earth, fourteen days was nothing. You planned a vacation for fourteen days. On Mars, fourteen days was the margin between breathing and not breathing, and it was the kind of margin that kept an engineer awake at oh-three-hundred, staring at a sheet of graph paper and running the same calculation for the seventh time, hoping the numbers would change because they were not changing.

They weren't. The numbers had been the same each morning for a week. Same input. Same output. Same deficit. Same reserve declining by six hundred liters every twenty-four hours, the way a wound bleeds at a steady rate that tells you everything about the severity and nothing about the solution.

Arun traced the reserve depletion curve on the graph paper — a line sloping downward from upper left to lower right, crossing the zero axis at approximately Sol 247, which was fourteen days from today. The line was straight because the deficit was constant. The line didn't waver because physics didn't care about hope.

He set the pen down and looked up at the ceiling, at the sensor camera that represented Mission AI's presence in the engineering bay. The camera was just a lens and a housing. It didn't think in the human sense. It processed. It computed. It modeled. But the AI's voice — the voice that filled the bay when it spoke through the overhead speakers — carried a quality that Arun had come to recognize not as emotion, because it wasn't, but as attention. The kind of attention a system gives to parameters when those parameters matter.

"Run it again," Arun said. "Full projection. Current MOXIE output, current consumption, no change."

"Running." Two seconds. "Current trajectory reaches zero reserve on Sol 247, fourteen days from today. On that date, the colony's oxygen supply consists entirely of MOXIE output. If MOXIE output remains at three hundred liters per day, consumption exceeds production by six hundred liters per day. The colony begins accumulating a respiratory deficit. Symptoms — elevated heart rate, decreased cognitive function, increased fatigue — appear within approximately forty-eight hours of sustained deficit. Cognitive decline impairs crew performance across all systems. System failures increase. The compounding effect of degraded crew performance and degraded systems accelerates the timeline."

"How quickly?"

"Full respiratory system failure within approximately seven days of the reserve reaching zero. That estimate assumes no emergency conservation measures. If conservation measures are implemented — reduced EVA, lowered activity levels, decreased greenhouse temperature to reduce plant respiration — the timeline extends by approximately three to five days."

"Three to five days." Arun repeated the number like a man repeating a diagnosis he didn't want to hear. "Maximum extension: nineteen days from today."

"Correct."

"And if the MOXIE output is increased?"

"If MOXIE output is increased to match consumption — nine hundred liters per day — the reserve depletion stops. The colony reaches equilibrium. Breathing continues indefinitely, assuming no further changes in consumption or production."

"And if we can increase it beyond nine hundred?"

"If MOXIE output exceeds consumption — say, one thousand two hundred liters per day — the colony begins rebuilding its reserve. The rate of rebuilding depends on the surplus. A three-hundred-liter-per-day surplus refills the eight-hundred-forty-liter reserve in approximately three days. A larger surplus rebuilds faster."

Aran sat quiet for a moment, absorbing the architecture of the problem. It wasn't complicated. It was an equation: production must equal or exceed consumption. Production was three hundred. Consumption was nine hundred. The gap was six hundred. The reserve was eight hundred forty. The reserve covered the gap for fourteen days. After fourteen days, the gap became a crisis.

Simple. Brutal. The kind of simplicity that made the problem feel solvable and the brutality that made the solving urgent.

He picked up the pen and wrote on the graph paper, next to the depletion curve: *Safe for now. Not safe forever.*

He underlined it. Not because it was a headline. Because it was the truth of the colony's position on Sol 233 — stable, but fragile. The stability was real. The fragility was real too. Both could be true simultaneously. That was the thing about living on Mars: every good day contained a seed of a bad day, and every bad day contained the possibility of a solution if you found it fast enough.

"Mission AI," he said. "I need to brief Elena in the morning. Give me the most concise version of this. Three sentences. No more."

"Current oxygen reserve: eight hundred forty liters. Current deficit: six hundred liters per day. Reserve depletion timeline: fourteen days, extendable to nineteen days with conservation measures. Solutions available: increase MOXIE output, reduce consumption, or both. Inaction guarantees respiratory system failure within three weeks."

"Four sentences," Arun said.

"You said three."

"I'm the engineer. I get four."

"Understood."

He folded the graph paper and slid it into his coveralls pocket. It would go on the wall in the engineering bay, next to the water board in the mess hall, becoming another number the crew looked at on the way to breakfast. Not the water number. The air number. Different parameter. Same architecture: a finite reserve, a growing deficit, a timeline that was counting down with every breath every person took.

Breathing was automatic. On Mars, it was calculated. Every breath the crew drew was a quantity that had to be accounted for, and the accounting was Arun's job.

He stood, stretched, and began the walk back to his bunk. The corridor was dimly lit — base lighting on its nighttime schedule, reduced to twenty percent of daytime brightness to conserve power. His footsteps were the only sound, and the rhythm of them — steady, methodical, unhurried — was the rhythm of a man who had accepted the weight of a problem and was preparing to carry it.

## Scene 2

The morning briefing was in the mess hall, the same room where Elena had held the water debrief three weeks ago. The geometry was the same — Elena at the front, crew facing her, a whiteboard mounted on the wall — but the whiteboard today held different numbers. Not water. Air.

Arun stood beside the board with a tablet, and the board displayed the atmospheric composition figures that Mission AI reported daily, printed in large, bold letters so everyone could read them from their seats.

Outside this base, on the surface of Mars, the atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide.

The numbers on the board:

CO₂: 95.3%
N₂: 2.7%
Ar: 1.6%
O₂: 0.13%

"Carbon dioxide makes up about ninety-six percent of the air outside," Arun said, and his voice was the measured voice of someone explaining something the crew already knew, because he knew that repetition was not redundancy — it was reinforcement. People who heard something every day stopped hearing it. Repetition forced them to hear it again, freshly, as if the first time.

"Carbon dioxide. CO₂. One carbon atom, two oxygen atoms. The carbon is useless to us — we don't metabolize carbon. The oxygen is exactly what we need. But the carbon dioxide molecule is stable. The oxygen is locked up inside it, chemically bound to carbon, and it doesn't come free. We can't breathe carbon dioxide because our lungs are not designed to break molecules apart. Our lungs are designed to take oxygen from the air and put it into our blood, and to take carbon dioxide from our blood and put it into the air. They are organs of exchange, not orga

ns of chemistry."

He paused. Laila, sitting in the front row, nodded slightly. She understood the distinction better than most people — the difference between biology and chemistry, between what a body could do and what a machine had to do.

"Inside this habitat," Arun continued, "the air is approximately twenty-one percent oxygen, four percent carbon dioxide, and the rest mostly nitrogen. That's the composition we need. The nitrogen is inert — it doesn't participate in our respiration, but it dilutes the oxygen to a safe concentration and provides atmospheric pressure. The oxygen is what we use. The carbon dioxide is what we exhale. We take in oxygen-rich air, we use the oxygen, we exhale carbon dioxide, and the exhaled CO₂ has to go somewhere."

He tapped the board.

"Every person in this room exhales approximately one kilogram of carbon dioxide per day. Thirty people means approximately thirty kilograms of CO₂ per day that the life support system has to manage. Most of it is scrubbed — removed from the air by chemical absorbents and converted into forms that can be stored or repurposed. But some of it accumulates, and the crew's comfort and cognitive function depend on keeping CO₂ levels below approximately five thousand parts per million."

A few people shifted in their seats. They knew the feeling of a space with high CO₂ — the drowsiness, the fog, the feeling of thinking through cotton — because they had experienced it in modules where the scrubbers faltered or the air cycling was uneven.

"The point," Arun said, "is that the air outside is not the air inside. Outside is ninety-six percent CO₂. Inside is twenty-one percent oxygen. The air outside is not wrong — it's just not for us. It's the air Mars produces. We are not adapted to it. But chemistry is not adapted either. Chemistry is a tool. And chemistry can take carbon dioxide — which we cannot breathe — and split it into oxygen — which we can — if we have machines and power and the willingness to build them."

He stepped away from the board and faced the crew directly.

"This is not a mystery. NASA proved it works. A MOXIE unit on the Perseverance rover produced oxygen from Martian atmosphere on Mars in 2021. We brought two full-scale MOXIE units with the original cargo. They work. But they work at a specific scale — a scale that, right now, is not enough."

He let that sink in. The crew already knew that MOXIE output was below consumption. They had felt it in the air — a subtle, creeping wrongness that no instrument measured directly but everyone noticed, the way you notice a room getting stuffy before the thermometer confirms it. They had seen the water board. Now they were seeing the air board. The same architecture. The same countdown.

"I'm going to show you the numbers," Arun said. And he did — the same numbers he'd been reviewing at oh-three-hundred, presented in a format the crew could read at a glance.

Production: 300 liters/day.
Consumption: 900 liters/day.
Reserve: 840 liters.
Days until depletion: 14.

He didn't add commentary. He didn't need to. The numbers were their own commentary — four lines of text that described the boundary between breathing and not breathing.

"That's where we are," Arun said. "Safe for now. Not safe forever. I'm going to talk about solutions. But first I need everyone to understand that the problem is not whether Martian air can be made useful. The chemistry works. The question is whether we can do it fast enough and at a large enough scale to matter."

He sat down. Elena stepped forward.

"I know this is a lot," she said. "I know it feels like the air is the one thing you take for granted. The one thing you shouldn't have to think about. I'm telling you to think about it, not because I want to worry you, but because air is the resource everyone assumes is stable until it isn't, and by the time it isn't, it's too late to fix it. This briefing is not an alarm. It's preparation. Arun will present the options. We will choose one. We will act. That is the plan."

She looked at the crew. Thirty faces — some alert, some tired, all listening.

"Questions now or later?" she asked.

"Later," said Laila, and a few people nodded. Processing first. Questions second.

Elena nodded. "Arun. Options."

## Scene 3

The MOXIE units sat in the workshop — the same cramped, overstretched space that served as engineering bay, fabrication shop, and emergency staging area for half the colony's operations. Two identical assemblies, each approximately the size of a large filing cabinet, constructed from stainless steel housings, ceramic electrolysis stacks, thermal insulation blankets, and a network of pipes and valves that connected them to the colony's air intake and oxygen storage lines.

They looked exactly like what they were: hardware designed for one purpose, installed on a planet where every other purpose competed for the same space and attention.

Arun knelt beside the left-hand unit, his hand on the housing near the main access panel. The unit was warm through the metal — not hot, but warm, the way a running engine is warm, the temperature of a system doing its job but doing it under strain.

"This is Unit One," he said to the small group gathered around him — Elena, Laila, Jonah, and Gabriel, who had come to record because every major system briefing needed a record, and the MOXIE units were about to become the most important pieces of hardware on the colony.

"Unit One has been running since Sol 12," Arun continued. "Output is approximately one hundred seventy liters per day. Design target was two hundred twenty-five. The shortfall is due to electrolyte membrane degradation — the solid zirconia membrane inside the ceramic cells has developed reduced ion conductivity, possibly from trace contaminants in the feed air that bypassed the desiccant bed. Output is declining at approximately two percent per week."

He moved to the right-hand unit.

"Unit Two has been running since Sol 18. Output is approximately one hundred thirty liters per day. Design target was also two hundred twenty-five. The shortfall is due to thermal management — the cells need to operate at approximately seven hundred fifty degrees Celsius for efficient solid oxide electrolysis, and the thermal system is struggling to maintain temperature during cold cycles when external temperature drops below minus seventy and heat loss through the insulation exceeds the heaters' capacity."

He stood and faced the group.

"Combined output: three hundred liters per day. Combined design output: four hundred fifty. We are operating at sixty-seven percent of design capacity. And the sixty-seven percent is declining — slowly, but declining. Unit One's membrane degradation continues. Unit Two's thermal issue worsens with each cold cycle. At current degradation rates, total output will fall below two hundred liters per day within approximately thirty days."

Laila spoke first — the physician's instinct, always the first to connect system performance to biological impact.

"What happens when output falls below two hundred?" she asked.

"The deficit increases. Instead of six hundred liters per day below consumption, the deficit becomes seven hundred or more. The reserve depletes faster. The timeline shortens from fourteen days to approximately ten to twelve."

"Which is unacceptable," Elena said.

"It is," Arun agreed. "Which brings us to the options. Option one: repair the existing units. Replace Unit One's electrolyte membrane, improve Unit Two's insulation and heater capacity. Option two: build a bigger system from parts we have. Option three: both — repair existing and build new, in parallel."

Jonah stepped closer to the units, his hand resting on the housing of Unit One the way Arun's had been — feeling, assessing, the builder's equivalent of a diagnostic.

"What's wrong with option two?" Jonah asked. "Build a bigger system. We have MOXIE technology. We have spare parts. We have a workshop. What stops us from scaling up?"

Arun looked at Elena. Elena looked at Arun. They'd had this conversation already — not about whether scaling was possible, but about what scaling cost.

"Parts," Arun said. "To build a scaled-up system that produces six hundred to nine hundred additional liters per day — the amount we need to close the deficit — we need ceramic electrolysis cells, zirconia membranes, high-temperature seals, thermal insulation. We have some of these in the spare parts inventory. Not enough for a full-scale build. We can make it work with what we have, but the system will not be robust. It will be marginal — running close to its limits, operating with reduced safety margin, requiring constant monitoring and maintenance."

"Robustness is a luxury," Jonah said. "We don't need robust. We need functional. If we can build something that works, even something that works barely, we buy time. Time to get more robust once the crisis is past. You don't build the perfect system when you're at fourteen days. You build the system that keeps people breathing. You perfect it later."

Laila considered this from her angle. "Medically, I can tell you that the difference between a perfectly safe oxygen supply and a marginally adequate one is the difference between comfort and survival. I would rather have marginally adequate oxygen today than perfectly adequate oxygen in three weeks when we've passed zero reserve. Perfection and survival are not compatible on a timeline this compressed. Build the system. Whatever system you can build. We'll manage the medical risk."

Elena nodded slowly. She had been listening to each person from their own perspective — engineer, builder, physician — and each perspective led to the same conclusion.

"Option three," she said. "Repair existing, build new, do both. Jonah — what do you need from me to make the workshop your primary workspace?"

"Time. Space. Priority on robot labor for heavy tasks. And I need Arun on the thermal design because the original MOXIE units had thermal management as their primary constraint, and whatever we build, heat is going to be the thing that tries to kill it."

"You have the workshop. You have the priority. Imani," she said, turning to the pilot who had entered the workshop unnoticed, "I need you running the water extraction survey so Arun can help Jonah with the build. Can you manage the GPR ground validation with reduced engineering support?"

Imani nodded. "Survey is mostly autonomous. I need Arun for drill calibration and sample analysis. That's two hours a day. The rest I can handle."

"Done." Elena turned to Arun. "How long to repair Unit One's membrane?"

"Two days. If I have the parts. If I don't, I'll need to fabricate a replacement from available zirconia stock, which takes longer."

"And Unit Two's thermal fix?"

"One day. Better insulation, upgraded heater element. Straightforward."

"And the new build?"

"Arun and I working together, full-time, with robot support — five to seven days. Depends on the design."

"Then we start today." She looked around the workshop, at the two existing MOXIE units sitting side by side on their concrete pads like a pair of aging athletes, still running but showing their wear. "Repair what we have. Build what we need. And Jonah — Arun — I want both of you in my office tomorrow morning with a design brief and a parts list. I need to know where we are on both tracks before the day is out."

She turned to leave, then paused in the doorway.

"One more thing," she said. "While you're building this, while you're calculating thermal loads and electrolyte conductivities and everything else that goes into a machine making air — don't forget why you're building it. Three weeks from now, someone in this room is going to notice that the air has gotten thin. That is the failure state I am trying to prevent. Not dramatic. Not sudden. Just a room that gets stuffy and then gets sleepier and then gets dangerous. You are building against that."

She left. The workshop door closed behind her, and the four of them — Arun, Jonah, Laila, and Gabriel — stood in the quiet hum of the two existing MOXIE units, listening to the faint electrical vibration of machines splitting carbon dioxide into oxygen and carbon monoxide, doing their job at sixty-seven percent capacity and declining, while the people responsible for fixing them were already thinking about the bigger machine they needed to build alongside the repair work.

Laila was the next to leave — she had patients to check, plant stress to monitor, the usual morning clinical rounds that occupied her regardless of whether the colony was in crisis. She paused at the door.

"Tell me when the first unit starts producing more air," she said, not looking back, already thinking about CO₂ levels, about cognitive thresholds, about the medical parameters she tracked when the environment grew thin. "Not because I need to celebrate. Because I need to adjust my monitoring baseline to the new normal."

"Will do," Arun said.

She left.

Gabriel stayed, recorder running, capturing the moment when two engineers stood in a workshop surrounded by the machines that made the air they were breathing, preparing to build a bigger machine that would make more of it, while the air in the room — twenty-one percent oxygen, four percent carbon dioxide, the rest nitrogen — continued its silent, steady cycling through lungs and scrubbers and MOXIE outlets, a cycle that had been stable until yesterday and would need to be stable for a long time.

Arun and Jonah began the work — Arun pulling up the technical specifications for Electrolyte membrane replacement on his tablet, Jonah surveying the workshop inventory for components they could repurpose for the scaled-up system, the two of them speaking in the shorthand of engineers who shared a workspace and understood both the constraints and the possibilities.

"This zirconia stock," Jonah said, holding a ceramic disc the size of a dinner plate, pale yellow, fired smooth. "How much membrane can we mill from this?"

"Approximately three membranes at the required thickness," Arun said. "But milling zirconia without cracking it requires precision tooling we might not have. I'll need to test a sample first."

"Test now. If it cracks, we know before we commit the whole disc. If it doesn't, we mill three and hope one is good enough for Unit One."

"If one is good enough, we install it and Unit One goes back to design output. That's two hundred twenty-five liters per day. Adds fifty-five to current production. Doesn't solve the problem. But it slows the depletion."

"Fifty-five liters slows the timeline by a day. Maybe two. A day is meaningful. Two days is meaningful."

"It's a margin," Arun said. "Not a solution."

"Margins are solutions when the timeline is this short," Jonah said, and began setting up the milling jig.

Gabriel watched them work — the engineer and the builder, operating in the cramped workshop that had become the colony's most critical room, surrounded by machines that split air into breathable and unbreathable components, surrounded by spare parts and hand tools and the kind of improvised connections that defined the colony's approach to everything: build what you can, fix what you must, accept what you can't change, and never stop working on the gap.

He didn't speak. He just recorded — the sound of the milling machine starting up, the high whine of the spindle, the rhythmic vibration of ceramic being shaped, the voices of two men talking about thickness tolerances and membrane conductivity while the air they breathed cycled through the units beside them and out into the habitat, and every liter of it was a small act of defiance against a planet's thin, unbreathable sky.

## Scene 4

Jonah found the compressors in the cargo module — two industrial-grade air compressors imported with the original supply shipment, designed for inflating the large atmospheric habitat panels during the initial landing phase. After landing, they had been used once, then stored because the habitat was inflated and didn't need reinflating. They had sat in the cargo module for months, sealed in their protective covers, unused but fully operational.

They were not designed for MOXIE feed air — they were designed for moving atmospheric volume, not maintaining precise flow rates at specific pressures through a chemical processing unit. But Jonah saw something in them that an engineer looking for replacement parts might have missed: raw mechanical capacity.

"These are good for approximately three hundred liters per minute displacement," Jonah said, running a hand along the compressor housing. Cast iron, greased, solid. The kind of heavy industrial hardware that was overbuilt by intention and had survived the journey from Earth in the same condition because it was designed for conditions harder than a supply ship's cargo hold. "We can use them to pressurize the feed intake to the new MOXIE stack. Right now, the existing units pull atmospheric CO₂ at ambient pressure — approximately six hundred pascals on Mars. If we compress the feed to twelve hundred pascals, we double the inlet density, which doubles the mass flow through the cells at the same volumetric rate. More mass flow means more oxygen production. It's the simplest multiplier we have."

Arun looked at the compressors, then at the MOXIE specs on his tablet, running the calculation Jonah had just described. It was sound — not elegant, not a textbook solution, but sound in the way that matters: the physics worked.

"Compressed feed. Double the density. At the same cell temperature and voltage, we'd get approximately double the yield." Arun ran the numbers on his tablet. "But the compressors draw power. The existing MOXIE units already pull eighteen kilowatts combined — that's significant against our one hundred sixty kilowatt surplus. Adding two compressors is another three to four kilowatts. We need to find the power."

"Take it from non-essential loads," Jonah said. "Reduce greenhouse heating by two degrees. Reduce non-critical lighting to twenty percent. Shift workshop heating to waste heat from the Sterling Generator. We're not talking about a lot of power — three to four kilowatts is a rounding error on Earth, but here, it's the difference between building a bigger system and not building one."

Arun considered the trade-offs. Reduced greenhouse heating by two degrees — that would stress Mei's plants, which were already under water stress. But thermal stress from reduced heating was different from water stress. Plants could tolerate two degrees of temperature reduction for weeks — possibly months — with reduced growth rates but not mortality. It was a cost, but not a fatal cost.

"Elena's going to want to balance this against greenhouse needs," Arun said.

"She will. And she'll approve it, because oxygen is a constraint on everything including the greenhouse." Jonah was pragmatic — not heartless, but willing to make hard trade-offs because the alternative was no trade-offs, and no trade-offs was another name for collapse. "The greenhouse needs air. The oxygen plant provides air. If the oxygen plant fails, the greenhouse has no crew to tend it and no CO₂ scrubbers to manage the atmosphere. So the oxygen plant is upstream of the greenhouse. The greenhouse is a downstream beneficiary. You fund upstream before downstream."

Arun nodded. He was running the full energy picture in his head — MOXIE power, compressor power, the thermal load of a new build, the power draw of the repair work on Unit One and Two — and the numbers were tight but not impossible. It would require operating at the edge of the power budget, with zero margin for error, meaning that any additional load — an unexpected spike in greenhouse demand, a cold cycle requiring extra heating, anything — would push the colony into deficit.

"Margin is thin," he said.

"Thin margin is still a margin," Jonah said. "On Mars, thin is all we've got for most things."

He began pulling the compressors from their protective covers — heavy, each one requiring a hand truck and careful maneuvering through the cargo module door, down the connecting corridor, and into the workshop where the new MOXIE system would be assembled. The compressors clunked and rattled as they were unloaded, the sound of heavy machinery on Mars — a sound the workshop had not heard in weeks, not since the water processing build had been completed and the equipment had been moved to its permanent location in the utility corridor.

The workshop was already crowded — the two existing MOXIE units on their pads, workbenches covered with tools and parts, the water processing equipment still occupying one corner for occasional maintenance, and now two heavy compressors taking up floor space that had been designated as the assembly area for the new build.

Jonah stood in the center of it all and surveyed the room the way a conductor surveys an orchestra before the first note — taking stock, finding the rhythm, identifying where each piece needed to go.

"We need space," he said. "For the new stack. For the compressors. For the thermal system. For the oxygen storage connection."

"Where?"

He pointed to the far end of the workshop, a section currently occupied by spare parts shelving and a parked maintenance robot. "There. We clear that section. Move the shelving against the opposite wall. Relocate the robot to the maintenance bay. We have approximately four square meters of clear floor space — enough for a scaled-up stack with access on both sides and room for the compressors at one end."

"Four square meters." Arun was already running the layout in his head — a larger stack than the existing units, built from whatever ceramic cells and zirconia membranes they could mill and salvage, plumbed to the compressors for feed, connected to the thermal system, output routed to existing oxygen storage. "That's tight but doable. The stack will be smaller than design spec — we don't have enough cells for a full production unit. We need to build a hybrid: part original MOXIE specification, part improvised. Cells we have, membranes we can mill, seals we can fabricate, housing from spare steel plate, thermal management from whatever insulation we can source."

"Improvised but functional," Jonah said.

"Functional but marginal," Arun corrected. "The thermal design will be the constraint. Ceramic cells at seven hundred fifty degrees generate enormous heat. We need to manage that heat — not just to protect the housing, but because the cells need to maintain a specific temperature for proper electrolyte conductivity. Too cold, efficiency drops. Too hot, cells degrade."

"Then the thermal system is priority. I'll design it while you spec the cells. We parallel-track: I do housing and mechanical, you do cells and chemistry. We converge on the thermal interface in the middle."

"Converge," Arun said, and the word carried the weight of two people who knew how to work together — not in perfect synchronization, but in complementary tracks that met at the critical junction because they had done this work together before, during the water processing build, and had learned to trust each other's judgment without micromanaging each other's domain.

Jonah was already sketching the layout on a sheet of engineering paper — rectangles for the stack, circles for the compressors, lines for the plumbing, notes for the thermal system — the way a builder always started, not with the details but with the shape, the geometry of what was possible.

Arun began pulling up the cell specifications on his tablet — dimensions, power requirements, electrolyte conductivity curves, temperature operating limits — the way an engineer started, with the parameters, the boundaries, the numbers that defined what could and could not be built.

Above them, the workshop's fluorescent lights hummed at full brightness because the air quality monitors told the environmental system that CO₂ was rising — three people working in a closed space with two operating MOXIE units and the compressors drawing additional power, generating additional heat, consuming additional oxygen. The irony was not lost on Gabriel, who was recording everything and who understood that the workshop itself was a microcosm of the colony's air problem: air in, air out, people breathing, machines working, the balance that had to hold or everyone in the room would feel it.

"Gabriel," Arun said, not looking up from his tablet. "How long has it been?"

"Since what?"

"Since anyone stopped noticing the air. How long before it becomes noticeable again?"

Gabriel thought about the question — not the technical answer, but the human one. The answer people felt in their bodies, not in numbers on a screen.

"About three weeks," he said. "If nothing changes. That's when the deficit becomes enough that people start feeling it. The headaches first. Then the fatigue. By then it's harder to think clearly, and thinking clearly is what you need to fix the problem."

"Three weeks," Arun said. He was entering the cell specification data into a model, the tablet screen filling with curves and numbers. "Jonah — how long to build this thing?"

"If we work full time, seven days. Five if we don't sleep much."

"Five days to build. Seven days to commission and bring online. Twelve days total."

"Twelve days," Arun said. He looked at the depletion timeline — fourteen days. Twelve to build and commission. Two days of margin. Not much margin. But margin was margin.

"We need to move," Jonah said. "We need to start right now. The compressors are unloaded. I'm beginning the housing fabrication. You spec the cells. We meet at the thermal interface in six hours."

"Six hours," Arun agreed. He closed the first tab on his tablet and opened the second — the cell specification matrix, a grid of parameters defining what a ceramic electrolysis cell needed to function as an oxygen producer at seven hundred fifty degrees.

Gabriel stepped back from them, giving them space, the recorder still running but no longer capturing dialogue. Instead, it captured the sounds of work beginning — the hum of lights, the clatter of tools on workbenches, the squeak of hand wheels as Jonah adjusted a vice, the soft tapping of Arun's stylus on the tablet screen — the ambient soundtrack of a colony deciding to breathe for one more week.

## Scene 5

Elena approved the build at oh-eight-hundred that morning, after reviewing the parts list Jonah had compiled, the energy budget Arun had calculated, and the timeline that — even in the most optimistic scenario — left only two days of margin between the completion of the new MOXIE system and the depletion of the reserve.

The workshop would become the build zone. All non-critical activity would be relocated. Jonah would have full use of the fabrication equipment — CNC mill, welders, bending brakes, tube cutters — everything the colony had in terms of metalworking capability. Arun would work alongside him on the cell assembly and thermal system integration. Robot support would be allocated from the prospecting pool for heavy lifting and material handling.

The risk was clear: if the new system failed — if the housing leaked, if the seals failed, if the thermal management couldn't hold temperature, if the compressed feed overwhelmed the cells — they would lose time, power, and confidence.

Time: five to seven days of dedicated work that could not be recovered.
Power: approximately three kilowatt-hours per day of surplus power diverted from other systems, including greenhouse heating.
Confidence: the most intangible and most damaging cost. If the crew saw the workshop build as a failure — a desperate improvisation that didn't work — the erosion of confidence could affect every other project they attempted, because confidence on a small colony was a shared resource, not an individual one. When one system failed, everyone felt less certain about every system.

Elena understood this. She had been a commander long enough before landing to know that a leader's hardest decisions were not about choosing between good and bad options but about choosing between risks with different architectures of consequence.

"Approving the build," she said, standing in the workshop doorway, her hand on the frame the way a person steadies themselves before a jump. "Jonah, Arun — you have full workshop authority until completion. Ration the greenhouse heating by two degrees. Reduce non-critical lighting. All robot heavy-lift priority goes to the workshop."

She looked at the two engineers — Arun with his tablet and cell specifications, Jonah with his sketch and tools — and for a moment, she looked not like a commander authorizing a project but like a person standing at the edge of a decision that would determine whether her people kept breathing.

"If this fails," she said quietly, "I want to know immediately. Not after commissioning. Not after the first test run. If you see a problem that makes you think this system will not work, tell me. We can stop. We can pivot. We can try a different approach. What I need is honesty, not commitment to a plan."

Arun nodded. "Understood."

Jonah nodded too. He didn't say anything. He rarely said anything when given direct orders. He absorbed them, filed them, and acted accordingly. That was one of the things Elena valued about him.

"I'll check in every twelve hours," she said. "Not to micromanage. To monitor. If the crew starts feeling air quality dropping, I need to know."

"They'll feel it in about three weeks if we don't get this online," Arun said. "Headaches, fatigue, cognitive decline. Laila is already monitoring CO₂ levels in the sleeping modules. She'll flag anything that crosses the threshold."

"Then Laila and I are your early warning system. You build. We watch the air. If the air starts going wrong before you're done, we implement conservation measures and buy time."

"Understood."

She stepped out of the workshop. The door closed. The lights dimmed to conserve power while the environmental system cycled, and in that dim moment between departure and action, Arun and Jonah looked at each other across the cluttered workshop floor — two people standing in a room full of machines that made air, about to build another machine that needed to make more, knowing that the thing they were building was not abstract or theoretical or academic, but the most concrete thing possible: the continuation of breathing.

Jonah broke the silence. "Let's start."

He walked to the far end of the workshop and began clearing the space — moving shelving, relocating the maintenance robot, sweeping debris, marking the floor with chalk lines to define the build area. Physical first. Geometry first. Before cells or chemistry or thermal systems, the space needed to exist.

Arun sat at the workbench and began the cell specification work — calculating the number of cells needed to achieve the target output, evaluating the zirconia stock they had on hand, planning the milling sequence for the membrane replacements, mapping the power requirements and the connections to the compressors and the thermal management system. Digital first. Parameters first. Before fabrication, the numbers needed to work.

And Gabriel stood near the door, recorder running, capturing the beginnings of a build that would either keep the colony breathing or fail in a way that would shorten the timeline to a point the air in the room would begin to feel thin.

The sounds: chalk on concrete. A hand truck rolling. Tools clattering. A tablet stylus tapping. The hum of lights. The steady vibration of the existing MOXIE units, running at sixty-seven percent capacity and declining, doing what they could while the people who understood their limitations built something that could do more.

Air, made useful. Carbon dioxide, split into oxygen and carbon monoxide by machines in a workshop on a planet that had never had a single breath of breathable air until human beings brought the knowledge and the will to manufacture it.

Arun looked up from his tablet, caught Gabriel watching, and said — quietly, almost to himself — "If this works, the crew breathes for another six months at least. If it doesn't, we have two weeks. The math is simple. The work is hard."

Gabriel nodded and kept the recorder running.

"Every day we build is a day the air gets thinner," Arun said. "Not noticeably. Not dramatically. But measurably. And measurable changes, given enough time, become felt changes. Given enough felt changes, they become dangerous changes."

He set the tablet down, picked up a piece of zirconia stock — a disc of pale ceramic, smooth on one side, rough on the other, marked with measurements and cut lines — and turned it in his hands like a craftsman inspecting raw material.

"This is going to become part of a system that keeps thirty people breathing," he said, not to Gabriel, not to anyone, but to the material itself, to the object that embodied the gap between knowledge and application. "No pressure."

Jonah, at the far end of the workshop, heard the remark and called back without looking up. "It's Mars. There's always pressure. Atmospheric pressure is about six hundred pascals. That's the minimum we're dealing with. Everything else is on top of that."

Arun smiled — just a shift of the mouth, the engineer's version of a laugh — and went back to work.

Above them, the workshop's environmental sensor cycled its reading: oxygen at twenty-one point zero percent, carbon dioxide at four point two percent, both within acceptable range. For now.

The air was holding. The clock was ticking. And in the workshop, two pairs of hands were working on the machine that would need to hold the air a little longer.

---
